page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: The definition
lines: The compressibility factor Z of a gas is the
ratio of the actual molar volume of the gas to
the molar volume of a perfect (ideal) gas at the
steps.why: Z compares the real gas against the ideal gas under the same conditions, so the definition must say a ratio of the two molar volumes at the same temperature and pressure.
common_mistakes: Leaving out at the same temperature and pressure. Without the same conditions the ratio has no meaning.
Inverting the ratio: the actual volume goes on top.
steps.memory_tip: Z = real over ideal. The real gas is on top.
steps.margin_note: Either form of Z earns the mark; PV/nRT is the form used in calculations.

steps.label: The ideal-gas value

lines.text: For an ideal gas Z = 1 at all temperatures and pressures

lines: Z < 1: attractive forces dominate (the gas is more
steps.why: For an ideal gas PV = nRT exactly, so PV/nRT is exactly 1. Any measured Z different from 1 is a direct measure of non-ideal behaviour.
common_mistakes: Saying Z = 0 for an ideal gas. The ideal value is 1.
Swapping the Z < 1 and Z > 1 cases.
steps.memory_tip: Attraction pulls the gas inward, so the volume and Z drop below 1. Molecular size keeps the volume larger, so Z rises above 1.
steps.margin_note: Z = 1 is the marked point; the two inequality lines show understanding.

insider_note: Z = 1 for the ideal gas is the second mark — a definition that stops before the ideal value is only half an answer here.
